record.context_brief: Geometric flag orbits in convex polytopes
record.original_question: For which values of k and d does there exist a convex d-polytope with exactly k geometric flag orbits?

evidence.quote: Problem 27. For what values of k and d is there a convex d-polytope with k geometric flag orbits?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let P be a convex d-dimensional polytope in Euclidean space, and let G(P) denote its geometric symmetry group (the group of Euclidean isometries of the ambient space that map P to itself). A flag of P is a maximal chain F_{-1} ⊂ F_0 ⊂ F_1 ⊂ ⋯ ⊂ F_{d-1} ⊂ F_d = P of faces of P, where F_i has dimension i (and F_{-1} = ∅). The group G(P) acts on the set of flags of P; the orbits of this action are called the geometric flag orbits of P, and their number is denoted f(P).

Determine, for which pairs of positive integers (k, d), there exists a convex d-polytope P with exactly k geometric flag orbits, i.e. f(P) = k.
artifact.status_search_result: The cases k = 1 (regular polytopes, classified by Schläfli), k = 2 (existing only in dimensions 2 and 3, fully classified), and k = 3 (existing in dimensions 2 through 8, with full classifications in dimensions 5–8) have been resolved. The general question of which (k, d) admit a convex d-polytope with exactly k geometric flag orbits remains open for k ≥ 4.

status_evidence.title: Convex Polytopes and Tilings with Few Flag Orbits (Matteo)
status_evidence.snippet: Convex polytopes with up to three flag orbits have been classified; two-orbit convex polytopes exist only in two or three dimensions; three-orbit convex polytopes exist in dimensions two through eight.
status_evidence.claim: Classifications are known for k ≤ 3, but the general (k,d) problem is not fully resolved.
